SAPS hot seat on discipline collapse

By: Viewfinder | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
... the South African Police Service breaks its months-long silence on the disciplinary collapse which allows brutal cops to go unpunished.

Unique Selling Point:
Whistleblower from inside SAPS speaks abuse and cover-up at station level

Summary:
Viewfinder and Carte Blanche reported three exposés on police abuse and failure of police discipline. At each turn SAPS stonewalled our queries. Now, SAPS senior management appears willing to sit for a ROR interview. Other exclusive elements also makes this pitch strong: whistleblowers within SAPS being willing to be anonymously interviewed, and my access to data containing solid examples of repeat offenders left unchecked across SA (similar to Gabriels).

Further information:
Interview with SAPS HQ - After months of stonewalling Viewfinder and Carte Blanche queries about the prevailing trends in police misuse of force and the systemic failure of SAPS's internal accountability system, the police service has agreed to sit for an interview with Carte Blanche. This follows from our exposé on Sgt Gabriels and Col Adonis at Athlone SAPS. Getting SAPS to account during a recorded interview on the underlying dysfunction which gave rise to Gabriels' unchecked rapsheet of brutality cases is a significant opportunity.

Police officers blow whistle via anonymous interviews (exclusive) - former colleagues of Gabriels - have agreed to be interviewed. They will blow the whistle on the organisational culture within their stations, which pivots on management enabling problem officers by failing to reign them in / discipline them. They will also speak on behalf of "good" police officers throughout the country, whose work of serving the community gets made much harder by colleagues who abuse their powers, brutalise and managers who fail to curb such trends. These interviews will likely also contain direct appeals to senior management to put policy interventions in place to improve the situation on the ground by ensuring that bad cops and bad managers who cover for them are dealt with. The interviews can be wider ranging too, speaking about the realities and challenges of policing work in SA. Again, an opportunity for an exclusive. The first time in this investigation that police officers have gone on the record like this.

Database of repeat offenders (exclusive) - I have a database of police officers that, similar to Gabriels, have racked up multiple IPID findings for brutality against them. I have examples in each province in SA and a description of the complaints in each of these cases which led to disciplinary recommendations. This data shows that routinely - as happened with Adonis' failure to deal with Gabriels - these apparent repeat offenders get off the hook. I also now have access to government PERSAL data which we can use to verify a sample of these cops' employment status as at March 2021 i.e. to show that as suspected / supposed in the police disciplinary data, these cops remained on the job. This exercise / data has not yet been reported in any other reporting of mine, so would be exclusive here.

Retrospective - Viewfinder has done three segments on police abuses and non-accountability. Each contains strong investigative findings, case studies, and memorable moments. The first aired the recordings of a police disciplinary hearing whitewash, for a case wherein a 15-year-old boy was allegedly shot in the back by a police officer. The second was an exposé on torture in KwaZulu Natal and the third was the exposé on Sergeant Gabriels. The story will recap and bring viewers back up to speed with Viewfinder and Carte Blanche's consistent reportage on the issue, which has now finally prompted a right-of-reply from SAPS head office.

Case study - I hope that I will be able to get a case study of a victim who was assaulted by one of the cops on the repeat offenders sample mentioned above. Working a source for contact details for complainants in WC cases. But, if not we can interview one of Gabriels' other victims, the retired nurse reportedly punched in the face. Also, just a week or so after our Carte Blanche aired on Gabriels there was a woman badly beat up at Athlone SAPS. She is still scared of being interviewed but said we could use photos of her injuries and medical exam. It seems that Athlone SAPS acted quite quickly in this instance to discipline.

Update on Gabriels / Athlone - I propose that Gabriels case will be background and not the main focus of this story. We can bring viewers up to speed, and our whistleblowers will comment on the case and the previous report on Carte Blanche. But there are some developments: Gabriels appeared in court on Friday, for Nikkita Peters assault GBH case. His lawyer argued that media should be barred from the trial (I have a bad recording where his lawyer argues the "media coverage is very biased"), and the magistrate dismissed the application and allowed the media / me to stay. Our whistleblowers and SAPS HQ interview can also speak to the Gabriels case.

Press Release:


Cracks in the Façade
Police brutality - including allegations of torture - has been exposed in several Carte Blanche exposés in recent months. Now, a police insider breaks through the ‘blue wall of silence’, detailing the habitual brutality and non-accountability at their police station. “It takes someone that is evil to do what was done that night”, the whistle-blower says, detailing how a station commander’s refusal to discipline a notorious cop may have enabled the torture and murder of a suspect in January 2020. We take allegations of officers implicated in abuse and cover-ups to the SAPS head office in a continued quest for accountability.
Producer: Daneel Knoetze | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script:


VOICE OVER
For months, Carte Blanche and journalism unit Viewfinder have covered the human cost of police brutality in South Africa.

In August, we brought you the story of 15-year-old Damian Ahrendse, from Wesbank outside Cape Town, shot in the back - allegedly by police - in a case of mistaken identity.

Klarina Reed (from police disciplinary whitewash)
Yes, he was falling right there. And the blood was all lying there. He couldn't breathe. But what he actually was saying to her, the police shot, shot him.

VOICE OVER
In October, we reported from the notorious Glebelands hostel complex in Umlazi, outside Durban, where police were accused of involvement in a spree of political killings.

Zukiswa Fica
I simply cried because I knew that he was probably dead.

VOICE OVER
And, in January, we exposed the alleged torture of 36-year-old Adam Isaacs by police and soldiers in Athlone, outside Cape Town, after his arrest on drug-related charges.


Voice over (NEW)
Isaacs was one of hundreds of people arrested during joint operations between the army and police on the gang-ridden Cape Flats, between 2019 and early 2020. Isaacs died of his injuries in hospital days after his arrest.

VOICE OVER
A common thread ran through these stories: the failure by police management to discipline officers implicated in such crimes.

We revealed that the Athlone station commander’s failure to discipline a notorious cop against whom allegations were made -- Sergeant Giovanni Gabriels -- may have enabled the torture of Adam Isaacs.

But, the crisis in leadership and accountability in the police service goes all the way to the top. Last month, the president announced the 'early termination' of police commissioner Khehla Sitole’s contract.

VOICE OVER
Throughout this investigation, police management, and those implicated in the brutality and cover-ups, met our queries with silence.

Now, finally, the police’s code of silence has cracked. A former colleague of Sergeant Gabriels - accused of torturing Adam Isaacs on that fateful day in Athlone - has come forward.

Derek
Why did you join the police service?

Anonymous
I wanted to help people … and the police seemed the way to go because it's an organization that is there to protect and serve. It’s not at all what I thought it would be.

Derek
What was your reaction to the Carte Blanche exposé?

Anon
I was relieved. I was glad that he was exposed because it was about time that someone said something and not keep quiet.

Derek
What was the response of the station leadership after Adam's death?

Anon
Nothing. They turn a blind eye. It's too much paperwork so the violence just goes on and is a spiral that goes and goes, until eventually there's a bomb.

VOICE OVER
Police disciplinary data reveal ample examples of officers repeatedly implicated in brutality being left unpunished by their commanders. But, this is not a case of just a few bad apples. Last year it emerged in Parliament that commanders routinely refused to discipline officers, even where the police watchdog IPID concluded that misconduct allegations against them were probably true.

VOICE OVER
Brigadier Stef Grobler was a career cop and a former head of the police’s Anti-Corruption Unit. He says this sort of thing has been going on for decades.

Derek
Now brigadier, was it difficult to be a good cop to use the term in your day?

Stef Grobler
Yes, I think it was … if you have to report everything you see, that's not right, you get such a bad reputation that in many instances, it's just better to just look the other way. It's a subculture thing, they refer to it as the “blue wall of silence” sometimes.

Derek
What's the culture within your police station, when officers are implicated in violent crimes?

Anon
It's not spoken about it would be like a hush-hush swept under the mat

Derek
So what can you tell us about the group of officers implicated in torturing Adam?

Anon
They have a history of torture. Of vio­lence. It was like a game to them. The one police officer … he bragged about how Adam was tortured. It takes someone that is evil. To do what was done that night.

Link
In recent months the police service has been under pressure to account for poor discipline within its ranks. It’s not easy to get direct answers, but we have stayed on the trail

Voice
Major General Mathapelo Peters is the police’s head of communications

Derek
General what is SAPS response to Carte Blanche’s investigation of Sergeant Giovanni Gabriels and Athlone police management?

Derek
A basic question: is he still on duty?

Peters
I can confirm that the member is on duty, just for purposes of progress.

VOICE OVER
While the police continue to drag their feet on the discipline or suspension of Sergeant Gabriels, the community at his current posting -- the small west coast town of Lamberts Bay -- says his pattern of abuse has continued.

Wherever Gabriels goes, it seems, police officers are also speaking out.

Carte Blanche has now received an affidavit written by one of Gabriels’ West Coast colleagues, which expressed outrage at the failure of management to discipline or disarm him.

The affidavit also highlighted that cops who blow the whistle on abuse can expect to be victimised.

Derek
Why did you decide to speak out? There are distinct dangers.

Anon
Yeah, there is. You get targeted. But from what I've witnessed and what I've seen. There's no need to use torture. Not at all these other ways and means of doing things. You get taught other ways.

Derek
So how do you think Adam died?

Anonymous
I know that he was assaulted, he was kicked, he was hit, that the bag was put over his head sprayed with pepper spray and it.

Link
Suffocation torture known as tubing is associated with the apartheid police. But, watchdog records show that it persists to this day. In fact, complainants say that it’s been refined – that pepper spray is sprayed into a plastic bag and pulled tightly over the victim’s head.

Voice over
In October last year, in Umlazi, we spoke to Richard Nzama, who is one survivor of this terrifying method.

Richard Nzama
And then they took me here, where they put the tube and then forced me to put my head, see, with the tube, see, inside the water […] I’m still asking myself, how did I manage to, you know, to survive?

Derek
So, what will you do to address the question of torture, especially tubing, during interrogations?

Peters
If we are dealing with specific cases, then it becomes easy to trace and investigate. But if it's just a general statement that is being made, then we don't. We're not really sure where to look at.

VOICE OVER
But, the police’s use of tubing torture is not “a general statement”. We provided Peters’ office with a list of more than 1,300 case numbers related to tubing allegations registered across South Africa in recent years, cases for which discipline has been virtually non-existent. This list seems to have prompted the veil of silence to descend again. Her office did not respond.

Police top management has been in crisis for years, it is routinely unable to respond to some of the most pressing safety concerns of South Africans. Now the search for a new national commissioner is underway.

Derek
What message would you have for an incoming national commissioner?

Anon
Take a serious look at management at stations. To be more firm.

Derek
What should the new national commissioner prioritize to restore our confidence and restore discipline within the police service?

Stef
I think you've answered that discipline. They should improve discipline.

LINK
It’s not as if the police don’t know they have a discipline problem. Head office sent out a circular last year warning commanders to stop protecting their colleagues.

VO
The circular said that commanders who continued in the old ways -- taking little or no action to enforce discipline -- would themselves be departmentally charged.

Derek
A basic question, has any commander ever been disciplined for failure to act?

Peters
Look, I'll speak from a time when when the correspondence you've been referring to was issued in October. Since that time, we have observed that there has been an improvement in that space and as a result, we have not taken any steps against anyone.

VOICE OVER
We followed up, but Peters provided no evidence of this supposed improvement, or to back up claims that the police was doing everything power to ensure discipline is enforced. Commanders who cover-up for their colleagues still have little to fear, it seems.

Derek
If you could convey a message to the incoming intakes. New police officers. What would it be?

Anon
If you witness anything, speak. Don't follow in the steps of your maybe senior member or your colleague.

Promos - to voice

(VO)
Discipline in the police has been in slow decline. After months of investigation, we confront police head office to ask what it will do to stem the tide of abuse and cover-up. (11 seconds)

(VO) For months, the police closed ranks as evidence mounted of a systemic cover-up of torture and brutality. (Stef Grobler) It's a subculture thing, I like to refer to it as the … the “blue wall of silence” VO But, has this wall finally cracked? (Upsound) It takes someone that is evil. To do what was done that night. (21 seconds)

VO Evidence that “tubing” - one of apartheid most notorious interrogation techniques - persists within the police service today? [Upsound] It’s torture whatever you want to call it, and it should not be happening. [VO] But, will the police service act to hold the perpetrators accountable? (21 seconds)

It’s not easy to get direct answers, but we have stayed on the trail Voice Major General Mathapelo Peters is the police’s head of communications Derek General what is SAPS response to Carte Blanche’s investigation of Sergeant Giovanni Gabriels and Athlone police management? Derek A basic question: is he still on duty? Peters I can confirm that the member is on duty, just for purposes of progress. VOICE OVER While the police continue to drag their feet on the discipline or suspension of Sergeant Gabriels, the community at his current posting -- the small west coast town of Lamberts Bay -- says his pattern of abuse has continued. Wherever Gabriels goes, it seems, police officers are also speaking out. Carte Blanche has now received an affidavit written by one of Gabriels’ West Coast colleagues, which expressed outrage at the failure of management to discipline or disarm him. The affidavit also highlighted that cops who blow the whistle on abuse can expect to be victimised. Derek Why did you decide to speak out? There are distinct dangers. Anon Yeah, there is. You get targeted. But from what I've witnessed and what I've seen. There's no need to use torture. Not at all these other ways and means of doing things. You get taught other ways. Derek So how do you think Adam died? Anonymous I know that he was assaulted, he was kicked, he was hit, that the bag was put over his head sprayed with pepper spray and it. Link Suffocation torture known as tubing is associated with the apartheid police. But, watchdog records show that it persists to this day. In fact, complainants say that it’s been refined – that pepper spray is sprayed into a plastic bag and pulled tightly over the victim’s head. Voice over In October last year, in Umlazi, we spoke to Richard Nzama, who is one survivor of this terrifying method. Richard Nzama And then they took me here, where they put the tube and then forced me to put my head, see, with the tube, see, inside the water […] I’m still asking myself, how did I manage to, you know, to survive? Derek So, what will you do to address the question of torture, especially tubing, during interrogations? Peters If we are dealing with specific cases, then it becomes easy to trace and investigate. But if it's just a general statement that is being made, then we don't. We're not really sure where to look at. VOICE OVER But, the police’s use of tubing torture is not “a general statement”. We provided Peters’ office with a list of more than 1,300 case numbers related to tubing allegations registered across South Africa in recent years, cases for which discipline has been virtually non-existent. This list seems to have prompted the veil of silence to descend again. Her office did not respond. Police top management has been in crisis for years, it is routinely unable to respond to some of the most pressing safety concerns of South Africans. Now the search for a new national commissioner is underway. Derek What message would you have for an incoming national commissioner? Anon Take a serious look at management at stations. To be more firm. Derek What should the new national commissioner prioritize to restore our confidence and restore discipline within the police service? Stef I think you've answered that discipline. They should improve discipline. LINK It’s not as if the police don’t know they have a discipline problem. Head office sent out a circular last year warning commanders to stop protecting their colleagues. VO The circular said that commanders who continued in the old ways -- taking little or no action to enforce discipline -- would themselves be departmentally charged. Derek A basic question, has any commander ever been disciplined for failure to act? Peters Look, I'll speak from a time when when the correspondence you've been referring to was issued in October. Since that time, we have observed that there has been an improvement in that space and as a result, we have not taken any steps against anyone. VOICE OVER We followed up, but Peters provided no evidence of this supposed improvement, or to back up claims that the police was doing everything power to ensure discipline is enforced. Commanders who cover-up for their colleagues still have little to fear, it seems. Derek If you could convey a message to the incoming intakes. New police officers. What would it be? Anon If you witness anything, speak. Don't follow in the steps of your maybe senior member or your colleague. Promos - to voice (VO) Discipline in the police has been in slow decline. After months of investigation, we confront police head office to ask what it will do to stem the tide of abuse and cover-up. (11 seconds) (VO) For months, the police closed ranks as evidence mounted of a systemic cover-up of torture and brutality. (Stef Grobler) It's a subculture thing, I like to refer to it as the … the “blue wall of silence” VO But, has this wall finally cracked? (Upsound) It takes someone that is evil. To do what was done that night. (21 seconds) VO Evidence that “tubing” - one of apartheid most notorious interrogation techniques - persists within the police service today? [Upsound] It’s torture whatever you want to call it, and it should not be happening. [VO] But, will the police service act to hold the perpetrators accountable? (21 seconds)

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ... the South African Police Service breaks its months-long silence on the disciplinary collapse which allows brutal cops to go unpunished.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Whistleblower from inside SAPS speaks abuse and cover-up at station level
metadata.Summary: Viewfinder and Carte Blanche reported three exposés on police abuse and failure of police discipline. At each turn SAPS stonewalled our queries. Now, SAPS senior management appears willing to sit for a ROR interview. Other exclusive elements also makes this pitch strong: whistleblowers within SAPS being willing to be anonymously interviewed, and my access to data containing solid examples of repeat offenders left unchecked across SA (similar to Gabriels).
metadata.Further information: Interview with SAPS HQ - After months of stonewalling Viewfinder and Carte Blanche queries about the prevailing trends in police misuse of force and the systemic failure of SAPS's internal accountability system, the police service has agreed to sit for an interview with Carte Blanche. This follows from our exposé on Sgt Gabriels and Col Adonis at Athlone SAPS. Getting SAPS to account during a recorded interview on the underlying dysfunction which gave rise to Gabriels' unchecked rapsheet of brutality cases is a significant opportunity. Police officers blow whistle via anonymous interviews (exclusive) - former colleagues of Gabriels - have agreed to be interviewed. They will blow the whistle on the organisational culture within their stations, which pivots on management enabling problem officers by failing to reign them in / discipline them. They will also speak on behalf of "good" police officers throughout the country, whose work of serving the community gets made much harder by colleagues who abuse their powers, brutalise and managers who fail to curb such trends. These interviews will likely also contain direct appeals to senior management to put policy interventions in place to improve the situation on the ground by ensuring that bad cops and bad managers who cover for them are dealt with. The interviews can be wider ranging too, speaking about the realities and challenges of policing work in SA. Again, an opportunity for an exclusive. The first time in this investigation that police officers have gone on the record like this. Database of repeat offenders (exclusive) - I have a database of police officers that, similar to Gabriels, have racked up multiple IPID findings for brutality against them. I have examples in each province in SA and a description of the complaints in each of these cases which led to disciplinary recommendations. This data shows that routinely - as happened with Adonis' failure to deal with Gabriels - these apparent repeat offenders get off the hook. I also now have access to government PERSAL data which we can use to verify a sample of these cops' employment status as at March 2021 i.e. to show that as suspected / supposed in the police disciplinary data, these cops remained on the job. This exercise / data has not yet been reported in any other reporting of mine, so would be exclusive here. Retrospective - Viewfinder has done three segments on police abuses and non-accountability. Each contains strong investigative findings, case studies, and memorable moments. The first aired the recordings of a police disciplinary hearing whitewash, for a case wherein a 15-year-old boy was allegedly shot in the back by a police officer. The second was an exposé on torture in KwaZulu Natal and the third was the exposé on Sergeant Gabriels. The story will recap and bring viewers back up to speed with Viewfinder and Carte Blanche's consistent reportage on the issue, which has now finally prompted a right-of-reply from SAPS head office. Case study - I hope that I will be able to get a case study of a victim who was assaulted by one of the cops on the repeat offenders sample mentioned above. Working a source for contact details for complainants in WC cases. But, if not we can interview one of Gabriels' other victims, the retired nurse reportedly punched in the face. Also, just a week or so after our Carte Blanche aired on Gabriels there was a woman badly beat up at Athlone SAPS. She is still scared of being interviewed but said we could use photos of her injuries and medical exam. It seems that Athlone SAPS acted quite quickly in this instance to discipline. Update on Gabriels / Athlone - I propose that Gabriels case will be background and not the main focus of this story. We can bring viewers up to speed, and our whistleblowers will comment on the case and the previous report on Carte Blanche. But there are some developments: Gabriels appeared in court on Friday, for Nikkita Peters assault GBH case. His lawyer argued that media should be barred from the trial (I have a bad recording where his lawyer argues the "media coverage is very biased"), and the magistrate dismissed the application and allowed the media / me to stay. Our whistleblowers and SAPS HQ interview can also speak to the Gabriels case.
